newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN SHARES SEEN HITTING NEW HIGHS NEXT WEEK.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN SHARES SEEN HITTING NEW HIGHS NEXT WEEK.

text.p: South African shares, which came to life this week soaring to fresh peaks, are expected to resume climbing next week as the market continues to buzz with speculation about a cut in interest rates.

Analysts said on Friday that the burst of foreign and institutional buying over the past five days on the back of very bullish official May reserves data would continue, although the heady pace may give way to some consolidation.

"In the very short term the market is looking very strong but the sustainability depends on whether we get a rate cut sooner rather than later," said Piet Viljoen, a portfolio manager at Investec Asset Management.
Expectations of a reduction in the country's high interest rates, which have squeezed consumers and been especially felt in the retail sector, follow signs that the economy is cooling off.
Figures released last week showed a surprise slide in first quarter gross domestic product growth. This week car sales data for May revealed a sharp year-on-year fall.

But the jewel in the crown was the news on Monday of an unexpected 7.4 billion rand leap in gold and foreign reserves to a record 21.8 billion rand in May, suggesting to some that South Africa has armoury to defend the rand if needed without having to rely on high interest rates.

The news sent the all-share index to a new all-time peak on Thursday, which was being built on in Friday's trading session. Industrial stocks had by lunchtime on Friday surged over 220 points in total on the week.

General consensus on interest rates amongst economists is for a reduction in the third quarter, with a total of three cuts expected by June next year. South Africa's Bank rate is currently at 17 percent, after a one percentage point hike last November.
Analysts said the reserves boon had also smoothed some concerns over a possible flight of capital when exchange controls are eased on July 1 to allow private individuals to invest offshore.
"Foreign investors are also feeling more relaxed with the reserves," Willi Jonker, executive director of portfolio management at Norwich Investments told Reuters this week.

Analysts said although shares' upside was intact, spurred too by a rise in gold shares as bullion edged up to above the $343 level in the wake of a surge in platinum, there would be fewer buying opportunities next week.

"(The market's) had a good move and it will slow down and gather a bit of consolidation...Those people that haven't bought this week will have difficulty getting hold of stock," said Malcolm Chapman, general manager of Absa Asset Management.
Any major fall on Wall Street, although the Johannesburg Stock Exchange seems for now to have severed ties, could also cut short the recent run.

Another niggling worry was the continued spate of poor corporate earnings from leading industrial firms, the latest being food group Del Monte Royal Foods Ltd which on Friday warned of lower interim and year profits.
One of the country's biggest clothing groups, Foschini Ltd is also expected to post a slide in year earnings when it reports next Wednesday.
"The hope is that a rate cut will boost corporate earnings which will then become more positive towards year end," a dealer said.
Trading next week could also become more volatile ahead of the futures close-out in two weeks time, dealers said.
